title: Autoworld 40th Anniversary
excerpt: Forty years of automotive history, brought together inside and outside the museum.

sections.heading: The Esplanade Comes Alive
sections.text:
The first impression came before even stepping inside.

For Autoworld’s 40th anniversary, the Esplanade in front of the museum had been transformed into a large Cars & Coffee, with more than 450 cars gathering beneath the arches of the Cinquantenaire. Classics, youngtimers and more unexpected machinery filled the space in front of the museum, turning one of Brussels’ most recognisable landmarks into an open-air celebration of automotive culture.

The setting did much of the work.

With the Cinquantenaire rising behind the cars, even relatively familiar models gained a stronger presence. Yet unlike some of the larger concours events we had attended during the year, the mood remained remarkably relaxed.

It did not feel overly formal, nor particularly intense.

Visitors moved between the cars outside and the museum indoors, naturally spreading the crowd between the two spaces. That balance made the afternoon feel accessible and comfortable despite the scale of the celebration.

More than anything, it felt like a gathering.

A birthday rather than a spectacle.

sections.heading: Forty Years Under One Roof
sections.text:
Stepping inside changed the atmosphere completely.

Autoworld has evolved considerably since opening in 1986. The museum itself describes its early years as a much denser display of more than 350 vehicles, with relatively little dedicated lighting or interpretation. Forty years later, the emphasis has shifted towards scenography, storytelling and temporary exhibitions designed around the cars rather than simply placing them side by side.

That evolution is immediately visible.

The lighting, spacing and presentation give the collection room to breathe, and during the anniversary weekend the museum felt particularly polished.

The temporary “Autoworld 40 Years – Looking Back to the Future” exhibition brought back vehicles connected to more than 100 previous exhibitions, reducing four decades, 105 exhibitions and over 2,000 displayed cars to a deliberately eclectic selection of just 15 cars, two motorcycles and a Vespa. Among them were the Bugatti Type 35B, Lamborghini Miura, Ford GT40, Audi Sport Quattro S1 and Porsche 918 Spyder.

The existing Ferrari display also worked particularly well within that environment.

Rather than feeling like an anniversary exhibition trying to tell every story at once, the museum offered several layers of automotive history at the same time: pre-war machinery, racing cars, classics, modern performance cars and the temporary anniversary selection.

sections.heading: Four Cars for Forty Years
sections.text:
At the centre of the museum, however, four cars immediately changed the tone.

For one day only, Autoworld brought together a Ferrari Monza SP2, Ferrari Daytona SP3, Bugatti Chiron and Aston Martin Valkyrie as the headline supercar display for the anniversary celebration, representing four very different interpretations of the modern exotic car.

The Monza SP2 looks backwards, reinterpreting Ferrari’s open sports racers through the brand’s Icona programme.

The Daytona SP3 takes a similarly historical idea in another direction, drawing inspiration from Ferrari’s endurance-racing past while wrapping it around modern engineering.

The Valkyrie sits almost at the opposite extreme: a road car shaped by the aerodynamic thinking of a prototype racer.

And then there is the Chiron, visually calmer than some of the machinery around it, yet carrying the unmistakable presence of Bugatti’s W16 era.

Placed under Autoworld’s carefully controlled lighting, the four cars felt less like temporary visitors and more like a compact exhibition within the exhibition.

It was a simple idea, but an effective one: celebrate forty years of automotive history by placing some of the most ambitious cars of the present among the machines that came before them.

sections.heading: A Museum That Still Moves
sections.text:
Perhaps the best part of the anniversary, though, was that not everything stayed behind museum barriers.

Throughout the afternoon, Autoworld also brought three cars from its collection back onto the road: a 1966 Ford Mustang, 1989 Ferrari Testarossa and 1954 Cadillac Series 62 State Limousine. Visitors could ride as passengers as the cars left the museum and circulated through the Cinquantenaire.

That small detail captured the spirit of the day particularly well.

Outside, hundreds of privately owned classics and youngtimers were still doing exactly what cars were built to do: arriving, leaving, idling and moving through Brussels.

Inside, automotive history was carefully preserved and presented.

And between the two, a few pieces of the collection were temporarily allowed to become living cars again.

That balance made the anniversary feel unusually complete.

Historic without becoming static.

Modern without forgetting what came before.

Special without becoming inaccessible.

Compared with the scale of Chantilly or the exclusivity of London Concours, Autoworld’s 40th anniversary felt much more intimate, almost like a family gathering built around a shared interest in cars.

Forty years on, that may have been the most appropriate way to celebrate it.
